set1.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
set1.q: What separates a diagnostic test from a screening test?
opts: Diagnostic tests are for symptomatic individuals
Correct, and screening tests are for asymptomatic ones, which is why the same test can be either depending on whom it is applied to.
Diagnostic tests are for asymptomatic individuals
Testing the asymptomatic is screening; diagnosis addresses those with symptoms.
Diagnostic tests are always more sensitive
The distinction is about the population tested rather than about the test's properties.
Screening tests are always the gold standard
Gold standard tests tend to be expensive and invasive, which makes them poor choices for screening.

set1.io: Discuss accuracy of diagnostic tests
set1.q: What is the practical use of a receiver operating characteristic curve?
opts: Determining the prevalence of the disease
Prevalence comes from the population rather than from a test's performance curve.
Converting pre-test odds to post-test odds
That is done with the likelihood ratio, either mathematically or by nomogram.
Deciding whether to test in parallel or serially
That decision turns on urgency, cost and risk rather than on the curve.
Comparing alternative tests for the same diagnosis
Correct, since it displays the whole trade-off between true and false positives rather than a single pair of values.

set1.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set1.q: As a rule of thumb, what does a likelihood ratio of 0.1 do?
opts: Lowers it by about 30 percentage points
That is the rule of thumb for a ratio of 0.2 rather than 0.1.
Lowers the probability by about 45 percentage points
Correct, mirroring the 45 point rise given by a ratio of 10, which is why below 0.1 counts as strong evidence to rule the disease out.
Lowers it by about 15 percentage points
That is the rule of thumb for a ratio of 0.5, which gives only weak evidence to rule out.
Lowers it to one tenth of its value
The ratio multiplies the odds; the rule of thumb is expressed as a shift in percentage points.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: How should a screening campaign combine tests?
opts: Screen with a highly specific test, confirm with a sensitive one
That order would discard cases at the first step, which is what screening is meant to avoid.
Use the gold standard for screening
Gold standard tests tend to be expensive, invasive and not easily completed, which makes them unsuitable for screening.
Screen with a highly sensitive test, confirm with a highly specific one
Correct, because the first pass should miss as few cases as possible and the second should avoid committing healthy people to further investigation.
Use two tests of equal sensitivity
The strategy deliberately pairs complementary properties rather than duplicating one.

set1.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
set1.q: Which test should generally be performed first in a serial strategy?
opts: The one with the highest specificity
Correct, because it avoids unnecessary testing of people without the disease, unless another test is cheaper or less risky.
The one with the highest sensitivity
Leading with sensitivity is the screening strategy, confirming afterwards with a specific test.
The gold standard test
Serial testing exists partly to avoid going straight to an expensive or invasive reference standard.
The one the patient prefers
Acceptability matters, but the rule of thumb is framed around specificity, cost and risk.

set1.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
set1.q: What should be considered when two tests disagree?
opts: Which test was more expensive
Cost bears on which test to order rather than on how to interpret conflicting results.
Which test was performed first
Order matters in serial testing specifically, but the first question is which strategy was used.
Whether they ran in parallel or serially
Correct, because the two strategies do different things to the combined sensitivity and specificity, which changes how the disagreement should be read.
Which test the patient prefers
Patient preference bears on acceptability rather than on the interpretation of discordant results.

set1.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set1.q: How is the rule-of-thumb probability shift applied?
opts: It is added to the pre-test probability
Correct, which is why the same likelihood ratio produces a very different answer depending on how likely the disease was before the test.
It replaces the pre-test probability
The shift is added to the starting probability rather than substituted for it.
It is multiplied by the pre-test probability
The ratio multiplies the odds; the rule of thumb works by addition to the probability.
It is subtracted from the specificity
Specificity is a property of the test rather than a quantity the shift acts on.

set1.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set1.q: As a rule of thumb, what does a likelihood ratio of 10 do to the probability of disease?
opts: Raises it by about 30 percentage points
A rise of about 30 percentage points is the rule of thumb for a ratio of 5 rather than one of 10.
Raises it by about 45 percentage points
Correct, and the shift is ADDED to the pre-test probability rather than replacing it, which is why the starting point still matters.
Raises it by about 15 percentage points
That is the rule of thumb for a ratio of 2, which sits in the indeterminate band.
Multiplies it by ten
The ratio multiplies the ODDS; the rule of thumb expresses the effect as an addition to the probability.

set1.io: Discuss accuracy of diagnostic tests
set1.q: What is a gold standard test?
opts: The cheapest test that detects the disease
Gold standard tests are often expensive, which is one of their named limitations.
A procedure believed to identify the disease with certainty
Correct, with culture for streptococcal throat infection, biopsy for cancer, cardiac catheterisation for coronary disease and endoscopy for peptic ulcer as the examples.
The test with the highest positive predictive value
Predictive value depends on prevalence; the gold standard is defined by identifying the disease with certainty.
The first test ordered in any work-up
Alternative tests are often the initial choice precisely because the gold standard is costly or invasive.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: With a sensitivity of 99 per cent and specificity of 95 per cent, positive predictive value rises from 17 to 51 per cent as prevalence rises from one to five per cent. What does that demonstrate?
opts: The test became more accurate
Sensitivity and specificity were held constant, so the test's accuracy is identical in both scenarios.
Specificity rises with prevalence
Specificity is a fixed characteristic of the test and was the same 95 per cent in both cases.
Negative predictive value is unaffected by prevalence
It fell from 99.9 to 97 per cent across the same comparison, so it moves too, in the opposite direction.
Predictive value depends heavily on prevalence
Correct, and the test itself did not change: the same sensitivity and specificity produced a threefold difference in what a positive result means.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: How is prevalence expressed in the lettered cells?
opts: a plus b, over all four cells
That is everyone who tested positive rather than everyone who has the disease.
a over a plus b
a over a plus b is positive predictive value rather than the proportion of the population with disease.
a plus c, over all four cells
Correct, being everyone with the disease over everyone tested. It is also the pre-test probability in the population of interest.
d over b plus d
d over b plus d is specificity, calculated among those without the disease rather than across everyone.
set1.cite: Assigned reading: The Classic 2 X 2 Table

set1.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set1.q: A rapid antigen test has a sensitivity of 65 per cent and specificity of 96 per cent. What is its positive likelihood ratio?
opts: About 0.36
That is the NEGATIVE likelihood ratio for the same test, being 0.35 divided by 0.96.
About 16
Correct: 0.65 divided by 0.04 gives 16.25, so a positive result makes the infection about sixteen times more likely.
About 1.5
That would fall in the indeterminate band and would not match a specificity as high as 96 per cent.
About 0.65
That is the sensitivity itself rather than the ratio derived from it.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: Why are predictive values influenced by prevalence?
opts: They include both diseased and healthy people
Correct, because each reads across a test-result row, which mixes the two disease columns in a proportion set by how common the disease is.
They are calculated within a single disease column
That is how sensitivity and specificity are calculated, which is why those two are not driven by prevalence.
Prevalence changes the sensitivity of the test
Sensitivity is a fairly fixed characteristic of the test rather than a function of prevalence.
Prevalence alters the gold standard result
The reference standard classifies patients independently of how common the disease is.

set1.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set1.q: What does a likelihood ratio describe?
opts: How much a result changes the probability of the condition
Correct, and its great advantage is that it is not affected by prevalence, unlike the predictive values.
The proportion of tested patients who have the disease
That is prevalence rather than a property of the test result.
The probability that a positive result is correct
That is positive predictive value, which does depend on prevalence.
The reliability of the test on repetition
Reliability concerns reproducibility rather than how a result shifts probability.

set1.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
set1.q: Which question should be asked about a study of a new diagnostic test?
opts: Was the study published in a high-impact journal?
Journal standing is not among the questions named for appraising a diagnostic test study.
Did every subject undergo both tests?
Correct, alongside whether the study included a spectrum of patients and whether those conducting each test were blinded to the other's result. That means the new test and the gold standard.
How many authors contributed to the study?
The number of authors is not among the questions named for appraising a diagnostic test study.
Was the test developed commercially?
Commercial origin is not among the questions named, though conflicts of interest matter generally.

set1.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
set1.q: What does diagnosing disease require?
opts: A gold standard test in every patient
Gold standard tests are often expensive, invasive or unacceptable, which is why alternatives are frequently the initial choice.
The highest available sensitivity in every case
Which property matters depends on the clinical situation, and sensitivity and specificity are inversely related.
Testing every patient who presents
Ordering tests indiscriminately is explicitly among the things to avoid.
A reliable method of detecting its presence or absence
Correct, because the task is to identify who has the disease and who does not, and that is only as good as the method used to separate them.

set1.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
set1.q: What is the trade-off of serial compared with parallel testing?
opts: More tests used, but less time taken
Using more tests in order to save time describes parallel testing rather than serial testing.
Fewer tests and less time
Serial testing saves tests at the cost of time rather than saving both.
Fewer tests used, but more time taken
Correct, which is why the choice comes down to how urgent the diagnosis is against how costly or risky the tests are.
More tests and more time
Serial testing leads to less use of laboratory tests than parallel testing does.

set1.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
set1.q: What does parallel testing generally increase?
opts: Sensitivity and negative predictive value
Correct, so disease is less likely to be missed. How much sensitivity improves depends on how well each test catches the cases the other misses.
Specificity and positive predictive value
Those are what serial testing maximises, at the cost of sensitivity.
The prevalence of the disease
Prevalence is a property of the population rather than something a testing strategy alters.
The reliability of each individual test
Reproducibility of a single test is unchanged by how it is combined with others.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: What kind of characteristics are sensitivity and specificity?
opts: Fairly fixed characteristics of the test
Correct, which makes them useful when planning a screening campaign but less helpful when explaining to a patient what their own result means.
Characteristics that vary with prevalence
Predictive values vary with prevalence; sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test.
Characteristics of the patient rather than the test
They describe how the test performs rather than anything about the individual being tested.
Characteristics that change with each result
They are stable properties rather than quantities recomputed for each patient.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: How is negative predictive value calculated?
opts: True negatives over true negatives plus false positives
True negatives over true negatives plus false positives is specificity, read down the no-disease column.
True positives over true positives plus false positives
True positives over true positives plus false positives is positive predictive value rather than negative.
True positives over true positives plus false negatives
True positives over true positives plus false negatives is sensitivity, calculated down the disease column.
True negatives over true negatives plus false negatives
Correct, reading across the test-negative row, which is why it depends on how many diseased people were in the population tested.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: What is positive predictive value?
opts: The probability that someone with disease tests positive
The probability a diseased person tests positive is sensitivity, read down the disease column.
The probability that someone testing negative is disease free
The probability a negative result is truly disease free is negative predictive value rather than positive.
The probability that someone without disease tests negative
The probability a healthy person tests negative is specificity, a fixed property of the test.
The probability that someone testing positive has the disease
Correct, calculated as true positives over true positives plus false positives, which reads across the test-positive row.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: What is sensitivity?
opts: The probability a person without disease tests negative
That is specificity, the mirror property on the other half of the 2x2 table.
The probability a person testing positive has disease
That is positive predictive value, which reads the table the other way, from result to disease.
The probability a person testing negative is disease free
The probability that a negative result is truly disease free is negative predictive value.
The probability a person with disease tests positive
Correct, and read as a probability it runs from zero, identifying none of the diseased, to one, identifying all of them.

set1.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set1.q: Which criterion in the modified Centor score can score minus one?
opts: Absence of cough
Absence of cough scores one point, as do fever, tender nodes and tonsillar findings.
Age over 45
Correct: ages 3 to 14 score one point, 15 to 44 score nothing, and over 45 scores minus one, because the infection becomes less likely with age.
Temperature above 38 degrees
A temperature above 38 degrees scores one point, like the other three clinical criteria.
Tonsillar swelling or exudate
Tonsillar swelling or exudate scores one point, like fever, absent cough and tender nodes.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: Written in the lettered cells, what is positive predictive value?
opts: a over a plus c
a over a plus c is sensitivity, calculated down the disease column rather than across the test row.
d over c plus d
d over c plus d is negative predictive value, read across the test-negative row rather than the positive one.
a over a plus b
Correct, dividing true positives by everyone who tested positive, which is why the mix of diseased and healthy people in the population affects it.
d over b plus d
d over b plus d is specificity, a fixed property of the test rather than a predictive value.
set1.cite: Assigned reading: The Classic 2 X 2 Table

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: In that same study, 9,895 of 9,975 patients without ulcers tested negative. What is the specificity?
opts: 99 per cent
Correct, and note that the 80 false positives outnumber the 20 true positives, which is what will wreck the positive predictive value despite this high specificity.
80 per cent
That is the sensitivity in the same example, calculated from the 25 patients with disease.
20 per cent
That figure is the count of true positives rather than any proportion of the healthy group.
50 per cent
A specificity of 50 per cent would mean the test classified healthy patients no better than chance.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: A test has a positive predictive value of 85 per cent. What does that mean for a patient who tests positive?
opts: The test detects 85 per cent of people with the disease
That would be a sensitivity of 85 per cent, which answers a different question.
85 per cent of healthy people test negative
Eighty-five per cent of healthy people testing negative would be a specificity rather than a predictive value.
They have an 85 per cent chance of really having the disease
Correct, and this is why predictive values are the useful numbers at the bedside: they answer the question the patient is actually asking.
They have an 85 per cent chance of being disease free
That reading belongs to negative predictive value, and for a negative rather than a positive result.

set1.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
set1.q: Which statement captures how common and uncommon disease present?
opts: Rare diseases present typically more often than common ones present atypically
The relationship runs the other way, which is why the common diagnosis is considered first even when the presentation is odd.
Uncommon presentations of common disease beat common presentations of rare disease
Correct, and it is the reasoning behind thinking of horses rather than zebras, tempered by the reminder that no disease is rare to the patient who has it.
Common and rare diseases are equally likely at presentation
Common diseases occur commonly, which is what makes prevalence useful in prioritising a differential.
Atypical presentations always indicate a rare disease
An atypical presentation of a common condition is more likely than a typical presentation of a rare one.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: What happens to false positives when a disease has low prevalence?
opts: There are usually fewer of them
Fewer false positives relative to true positives is what happens when prevalence is HIGH.
There are usually more of them
Correct, because the pool of healthy people is so much larger that even a small false positive rate produces many of them relative to the few true cases.
Their number is unaffected by prevalence
The balance between true and false positives shifts directly with how many people actually have the disease.
They become true positives
Classification against the gold standard does not change; what changes is how many of each there are.

set1.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
set1.q: What limits the diagnosis of disease?
opts: The prevalence of the disease alone
Prevalence shapes what a result means but is not what limits diagnosis in general.
The number of tests ordered
Ordering more tests does not overcome the limits of the tests themselves, and indiscriminate ordering is to be avoided.
How good the tests used to measure it are
Correct, and the rest follows from it: sensitivity and specificity guide test selection, while predictive values describe what a given result means.
The cost of the gold standard
Cost affects which tests are practical rather than setting the limit on diagnosis.

set1.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set1.q: As prevalence falls, what happens to the two predictive values?
opts: Both fall together
They move in opposite directions, which is what makes prevalence worth knowing before a result is interpreted.
Both rise together
The two predictive values move in opposite directions as prevalence changes rather than rising together.
Positive predictive value rises and negative falls
That is what happens as prevalence INCREASES, when there are more true positive cases.
Positive predictive value falls and negative rises
Correct, because there are fewer true positive cases to be found, so a positive result is more often wrong and a negative result more often right.
set1.cite: Assigned reading: The Classic 2 X 2 Table

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: A test has a negative likelihood ratio of 0.5. What does a negative result mean?
opts: The patient is half as likely to have the condition
Correct, relative to the pre-test probability. A ratio below one lowers the probability, and one above one raises it.
The patient is twice as likely to have the condition
A ratio below one moves the probability down rather than up.
Half of all negative results are wrong
The ratio expresses a shift in probability rather than an error rate.
The disease has a prevalence of 50 per cent
A likelihood ratio is a property of the test result rather than a statement about how common the disease is.

set2.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set2.q: What does a sensitivity of 0.5 mean?
opts: Half the patients testing positive have the disease
That would be a positive predictive value of 0.5, which reads from result to disease rather than the reverse.
Half the healthy patients test negative
Half the healthy patients testing negative would be a specificity of 0.5 rather than a sensitivity.
The test is half as expensive as the gold standard
The scale from zero to one is a probability rather than a cost comparison.
An equal chance of identifying a diseased patient
Correct. A value of one identifies every patient with the disease, and a value of zero identifies none of them.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: A test has a positive likelihood ratio of 4. What does that mean?
opts: Four per cent of positive results are correct
The ratio is a multiplier on the odds rather than a percentage of correct results.
A positive result makes it four times more likely
Correct, relative to the pre-test probability, which is what makes the ratio a multiplier rather than a probability in its own right.
Four patients in every hundred have the disease
Four patients per hundred having the disease would be a prevalence rather than a likelihood ratio.
The test is correct four times out of five
A likelihood ratio does not express a rate of correctness; it expresses how much the result shifts probability.

set2.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
set2.q: What characterises parallel testing?
opts: Tests are conducted one after another
That is serial testing, which takes longer but uses fewer tests overall.
Only the gold standard is used
Parallel testing combines several tests rather than relying on the reference standard.
The most specific test is done first
Leading with the most specific test is the rule of thumb for SERIAL testing.
All tests are conducted at once
Correct, and it is used when rapid diagnosis is preferred, at the cost of running tests that serial strategy might have made unnecessary.

set2.io: Discuss accuracy of diagnostic tests
set2.q: Between what values must a probability lie?
opts: Zero and one hundred
A probability lies between zero and one; a percentage is that value expressed on a different scale.
Minus one and one
Probabilities cannot be negative, since an event cannot occur less often than never.
Zero and one
Correct, with zero meaning the event cannot occur and one meaning it certainly will. All the probabilities of events in a sample must sum to one.
One and ten
That range describes likelihood ratio bands rather than probability itself.

set2.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
set2.q: Why should those conducting each test be blinded to the other's result?
opts: Blinding increases the prevalence of the disease
Prevalence is a property of the population and is unaffected by blinding.
One result could influence the reading of the other
Correct, and it is a form of measurement bias: the test would then appear to agree with the standard partly because the reader expected it to.
Blinding is required for the likelihood ratio to apply
The ratio is calculated from sensitivity and specificity, however those were obtained.
Blinding reduces the cost of the study
Blinding protects against bias in reading the results rather than reducing the cost of the study.

set2.io: Discuss accuracy of diagnostic tests
set2.q: What limits the use of gold standard tests?
opts: They are often expensive and invasive
Correct, and they may not be acceptable to patients, which is why alternative tests are often the initial choice and are then compared against the standard. They may also be hard to complete.
They are insufficiently sensitive
They are believed to identify the disease with certainty; the problem is practical rather than one of accuracy.
They cannot be compared with other tests
Comparison against them is exactly how other tests are evaluated.
They are affected by disease prevalence
Prevalence affects predictive values rather than whether the reference standard identifies disease.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: What does a likelihood ratio below 0.1 indicate?
opts: Moderate evidence to rule out
Moderate evidence to rule out corresponds to the 0.1 to 0.2 band.
Strong evidence to rule out
Correct, and such a ratio virtually rules out the chance that the patient has the disease, which is the mirror of a ratio above 10 ruling it in.
Weak evidence to rule out
Weak evidence to rule out corresponds to the 0.2 to 0.5 band.
An indeterminate result
The indeterminate band runs from 0.5 to 2, well above a ratio capable of ruling disease out.

set2.io: Discuss accuracy of diagnostic tests
set2.q: What does validity mean for a test?
opts: Getting a similar result on repetition
That is reliability, also called precision, which says nothing about whether the result is right.
Its ability to change the post-test probability
That is what the likelihood ratio describes rather than what validity means.
Its cost relative to the gold standard
Cost is a consideration when ordering a test rather than a component of its accuracy.
Its ability to determine correctly who has the disease
Correct, and it is measured by sensitivity and specificity. Reliability, by contrast, is getting a similar result when the test is repeated under the same conditions.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: Why does post-test probability matter?
opts: It determines the sensitivity of the test
Sensitivity is fixed by the test rather than derived from an individual's probability.
It informs treatment decisions
Correct, and clinicians need an evidence-based but simple method of arriving at it, which is what the likelihood ratio and its nomogram provide.
It replaces the need for a gold standard
The gold standard is what the test was validated against; probability estimates do not substitute for it.
It is the same as the prevalence
Prevalence often serves as the PRE-test probability; the post-test value is what the result revises it to.

set2.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set2.q: In the classic 2x2 table lettered a to d, which cell is b?
opts: True positives
True positives are cell a, in the disease column of the test-positive row.
False negatives
False negatives are cell c, in the disease column of the test-negative row.
False positives
Correct: a is true positives, b false positives, c false negatives and d true negatives, reading across the top row then the bottom.
True negatives
True negatives are cell d, in the no-disease column of the test-negative row.
set2.cite: Assigned reading: The Classic 2 X 2 Table

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: How is the positive likelihood ratio calculated?
opts: Sensitivity divided by one minus specificity
Correct, which is the probability of a positive result in disease over the probability of a positive result without it.
One minus sensitivity, divided by specificity
One minus sensitivity over specificity is the NEGATIVE likelihood ratio rather than the positive one.
Specificity divided by one minus sensitivity
Neither ratio is built that way; the positive ratio puts sensitivity over one minus specificity.
True positives divided by all positives
That is positive predictive value, which varies with prevalence.

set2.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
set2.q: Why does it matter whether a test study's prevalence matches your own population?
opts: Sensitivity will differ if prevalence differs
Sensitivity is a fairly fixed characteristic of the test rather than a function of prevalence.
Predictive values will differ if prevalence differs
Correct, and that is the practical consequence of predictive values depending on prevalence: a published value may not transfer to your setting.
The gold standard will classify patients differently
The reference standard classifies patients independently of how common the disease is.
The likelihood ratio will change
The likelihood ratio is specifically not affected by prevalence, which is its chief advantage.

set2.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set2.q: Written in the lettered cells, what is sensitivity?
opts: d over b plus d
d over b plus d is specificity, calculated down the no-disease column rather than the disease column.
a over a plus b
That is positive predictive value, read across the test-positive row.
d over c plus d
That is negative predictive value, read across the test-negative row.
a over a plus c
Correct, since a is true positives and c false negatives, so the denominator is everyone who actually has the disease.
set2.cite: Assigned reading: The Classic 2 X 2 Table

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: How is the negative likelihood ratio calculated?
opts: Sensitivity divided by one minus specificity
Sensitivity over one minus specificity is the POSITIVE likelihood ratio rather than the negative one.
One minus sensitivity, divided by specificity
Correct, being the probability of a negative result in disease over the probability of a negative result without it.
Specificity divided by sensitivity
Neither ratio is a simple quotient of the two properties; each involves one of them subtracted from one.
True negatives divided by all negatives
That is negative predictive value rather than a likelihood ratio.

set2.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set2.q: What does a negative result on a highly sensitive test do?
opts: It rules disease out
Correct, remembered as SnOUT. A high sensitivity means few false negatives, so a negative result is unlikely to be missing the disease.
It rules disease in
Ruling in is what a positive result on a highly SPECIFIC test does, remembered as SpIN.
It establishes the post-test probability exactly
Post-test probability follows from the pre-test probability and the likelihood ratio rather than from sensitivity alone.
It has no interpretive value
A negative on a highly sensitive test is precisely the result that carries weight.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: Which range of likelihood ratios is indeterminate?
opts: Correct, because a result in that band shifts the probability so little that it leaves the clinical question roughly where it was.
The 0.2 to 0.5 band gives weak evidence to rule the disease out rather than no useful evidence.
The 0.1 to 0.2 band gives moderate evidence to rule the disease out.
5 to 10
The 5 to 10 band gives moderate evidence to rule the disease in rather than being indeterminate.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: What is pre-test probability?
opts: The chance of disease before the test is done
Correct, and it is often simply the prevalence of the disease in the population the patient comes from.
The chance of disease once the result is known
That is post-test probability, which is what informs the treatment decision.
The probability that the test will be positive
The quantity concerns the patient's disease status rather than the anticipated result.
The sensitivity of the test being ordered
Sensitivity is a property of the test rather than of this patient's likelihood of disease.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: Which tool is used to estimate the pre-test probability of streptococcal pharyngitis?
opts: The likelihood ratio nomogram
The nomogram converts a pre-test probability into a post-test one rather than generating the starting estimate.
The receiver operating characteristic curve
That curve compares tests rather than estimating a patient's probability of disease.
The modified Centor score
Correct, scoring temperature above 38 degrees, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical nodes, tonsillar swelling or exudate, and age.
The 2x2 table
The table yields the test's properties rather than an individual patient's pre-test probability.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: What does a likelihood ratio greater than one do to the probability?
opts: Lowers the post-test probability
Ratios below one lower the probability; those above one raise it.
Raises the post-test probability
Correct, and a ratio below one lowers it. A very low ratio, below about 0.1, virtually rules the disease out. It rises above the pre-test value.
Leaves the probability unchanged
A ratio of exactly one would leave it unchanged, which is why the indeterminate band sits around that value.
Converts probability into odds
Conversion to odds is a step in the arithmetic rather than an effect of the ratio's size.

set2.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
set2.q: What example is given of serial testing?
opts: Rapid antigen testing alongside throat culture
Running two tests at the same time is parallel rather than serial testing.
Endoscopy followed by a hypothetical upper gastrointestinal test
That order puts the gold standard first, which defeats the purpose of testing serially.
Biopsy repeated after an interval
Repeating one test is not a serial strategy, and repeating without indication is to be avoided.
Exercise tolerance testing, then catheterisation if positive
Correct, for coronary artery disease: the simpler, safer test runs first and the invasive one follows only on a positive result.

set2.io: Discuss accuracy of diagnostic tests
set2.q: What is true of the accuracy of diagnostic tests in general?
opts: A gold standard test is absolutely accurate
It is believed to identify the disease with certainty, but no test is described as absolutely accurate.
Accuracy has no bearing on interpretation
Accuracy is precisely what determines how a result should be interpreted.
Accuracy improves with repeated testing
Repetition addresses reliability, and repeating without indication is to be avoided.
No test is absolutely accurate
Correct, but accuracy still affects the probability of finding disease present or absent, which is why test quality has to be assessed before use.

set2.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set2.q: When does high sensitivity matter most?
opts: When a false positive would trigger risky further testing
That is when high specificity matters, since it produces few false positives.
When the test is expensive
Cost bears on whether to order a test rather than on which property to prioritise.
When missing the disease would have serious consequences
Correct, because few false negatives is exactly the property needed when the cost of overlooking a case is high.
When the disease is highly prevalent
Prevalence affects predictive values rather than which of the two fixed properties is more important.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: What is the mathematical route from pre-test probability to post-test probability?
opts: Convert to odds, multiply by the ratio, convert back
Correct, and the nomogram exists to spare the arithmetic: a line drawn from the pre-test probability through the ratio meets the post-test probability.
Multiply the pre-test probability by the ratio directly
The multiplication works on odds rather than on probabilities, which is why the two conversions are needed.
Add the ratio to the pre-test probability
The ratio is a multiplier on odds rather than an increment to a probability.
Divide the pre-test probability by the specificity
Neither quantity is combined that way; the route runs through odds and the likelihood ratio.

set2.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
set2.q: When is serial testing used?
opts: When a diagnosis is needed as quickly as possible
Needing a diagnosis quickly is the reason for parallel testing rather than for testing serially.
When every test is cheap and safe
Expense and risk are among the reasons to test serially rather than all at once.
When only one test exists for the condition
Serial testing by definition involves more than one test, applied one after another.
When speed matters less, or tests are risky
Correct, and it follows on after simpler and safer tests have proved inconclusive. Costly tests are another reason.

set2.io: Describe pretest odds, posttest odds and likelihood ratios
set2.q: What does a likelihood ratio above 10 indicate?
opts: Moderate evidence to rule in
Moderate evidence to rule in corresponds to the 5 to 10 band rather than to ratios above 10.
Strong evidence to rule in
Correct, with 5 to 10 giving moderate evidence to rule in, and the band from 0.5 to 2 being indeterminate.
Strong evidence to rule out
Ruling a disease out strongly requires a ratio below 0.1 rather than one above 10.
An indeterminate result
The indeterminate band runs from 0.5 to 2, where a result barely shifts the probability at all.

set2.io: Describe sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value
set2.q: What defines a false positive in a 2x2 table?
opts: The new test is negative and the gold standard positive
That is a false negative, which a highly sensitive test produces few of.
Both tests are positive
Agreement between the two tests on a positive result makes the patient a true positive rather than a false one.
The new test is positive and the gold standard negative
Correct, and false positives are what a highly specific test produces few of, which is why a positive on such a test rules disease in.
Both tests are negative
Agreement between the two tests on a negative result makes the patient a true negative.

set2.io: Describe parallel testing and serial testing
set2.q: What determines how much parallel testing improves sensitivity?
opts: How specific each test is
Specificity governs false positives, whereas the gain being described is in case detection.
How expensive the tests are
Cost bears on which strategy is chosen rather than on how much sensitivity improves.
How well each catches what the other misses
Correct: two tests that fail on the same patients add little, whereas complementary tests between them catch far more of the cases.
The prevalence of the disease
Prevalence affects predictive values rather than how complementary two tests are.

set2.io: Discuss accuracy of diagnostic tests
set2.q: What does a receiver operating characteristic curve plot?
opts: Positive predictive value against prevalence
That relationship is shown in the prevalence tables rather than by this curve.
Pre-test probability against post-test probability
That relationship is read from the likelihood ratio nomogram.
True positive rate against false positive rate
Correct, with one minus specificity on the horizontal axis, which lets clinicians compare alternative tests for the same diagnosis.
Sensitivity against disease severity
Severity is not one of the axes; the curve trades true positives against false positives.

set2.io: Identify and describe limitations of diagnostic tests
set2.q: Which considerations apply when ordering a diagnostic test?
opts: Risk against benefit, the test's limits, and its cost
Correct, alongside two instructions: avoid ordering tests indiscriminately, and avoid repeating a test without an indication.
Order the most sensitive test available in every case
Sensitivity and specificity are inversely related, so which matters depends on the clinical question.
Repeat every abnormal test at least twice
Repeating a test without an indication is specifically something to avoid.
Order every test the patient requests
Indiscriminate ordering is named as the first thing to avoid.
